Q: How to Debug Error 400: Bad Request? (PHP) A:

First of all you have to determine, who is responsible for this error: the web server or your PHP code.

  • for the web-server is's simple: there will be an entry error log. Check it carefully. You can grep the log file for 400 error specifically, like grep 400 /path/to/error.log. There fill be false positives of course but it will give you a starting point. After getting the actual error message from the log, you can google/chatbot it for the explanation and possible remedies. Like, sometimes PHP devs make a mistake that causes uncontrolled growth for a cookie value, which will eventually cause this error.
  • for your PHP code it's even simpler: there must be explicit code that respond with such error code, so you can search your codebase for "400" or look for functions like http_response_code(). After finding the place, you can add a more descriptive error message to making debugging easier the next time.

Another suggestion, which is less scientific but can be quicker is checking the Dev console in your browser. Since 400 is an HTTP response, it's a problem with HTTP headers. And in the Network tab of Dev console, after selecting the problem request, you can observe the headers and try to spot some abnormality. Such as same cookie size for example.

Q: Images not loading when hosting Next.js application on GitHub Pages A:

From what I have experimented with Next.js, when you use image optimizations, then paths for images are likely to change (due to Next.js optimizations).

So instead of hardcoding src attribute, you should import it instead:

import portrait from "/portrait.jpg"
...
<Image src={portrait} />

Here's example of my Next.js component, that is released here (all images are handled the same).

You can even observe how img element was produced:

<img alt="RSM" loading="lazy" width="357" height="150" decoding="async" data-nimg="1" style="color:transparent" srcset="/_next/image?url=%2F_next%2Fstatic%2Fmedia%2Frsm.8291421b.png&w=384&q=75 1x, /_next/image?url=%2F_next%2Fstatic%2Fmedia%2Frsm.8291421b.png&w=750&q=75 2x" src="/_next/image?url=%2F_next%2Fstatic%2Fmedia%2Frsm.8291421b.png&w=750&q=75">

You can test it in your example as well, without releasing anything, just by doing npm run build or equivalent command you defined for building your asssets.

And how it was defined in the source:

<Image height={150} src={rsm} alt="RSM" />

Word on image optimization (as it couldn't fit into comment)

This is not specific to Next.js. This is specific to any image optimization engines.

I would recommend reading

  • image performance,
  • Next.js image optimizations.

To say shortly - image optimizations are transforming original image to different sizes and formats in order to assure best performance. Image optimization can be separate from framework (eg. vite-plugin-image-optimizer, that can be embedded with Vite project with any framework), are can be included in framework, like Next.js, which you opt into by using Image component.

One case of image optimization is to also upload them to CDN. Then you img elements would refer to assets from CDNs, which clearly indicates you shold not hardcode srcs in your code.

Q: Waiting for child state with execl in C A:

When you don't call wait(), the parent exits immediately while the child is still running ls. This returns control to the shell, which displays a new prompt. The child's output then gets mixed with the shell prompt, making it look like the shell is "asking for input", it's just the prompt appearing before ls finishes

With wait(): The parent blocks until the child completes, so the output is clean and sequential

Without wait(): Race condition - patent exits -> shell prompt appears -> child output ls results

Best Practice: Always wait() for child processes unless you explicitly want them to run as background jobs. Otherwise you create zombie processes that remain in the process table until the parent recaps them

} else {   // parent
    printf("Parent (pid:%d), Child (pid:%d)\n", (int) getpid(), rc);
    wait(NULL); // Always wait for the child to prevent zombies
}

Q: Random generated string detection A:

One approach is to measure the likelihood of your text under some language model, possibly after some priming text ("prompt"). Since language models are trained on human text, they will naturally predict text sequences that are more likely to be produced by humans, and will therefore assign lower probabilities to text sequences that are somehow "not human". Any language model that is trained on enough text would work: it does not have to be an LLM, although you will probably get the most accurate results with an LLM.

As an example: given the priming text "The capital of Spain is ", the word "Madrid" would have very high likelihood, whereas the word "aisodjasjd92j23ewds" would have rather lower likelihood, and "8tBzVLlxVQGoCYs" would have even lower likelihood. (Note that because aisodjasjd92j23ewds was banged out on a keyboard, a large-enough language model is likely to be able to predict the later parts of the input with higher probability than pure chance).

You'll have to figure out a suitable prompt (you could, for example, try a very naive "The following word was written by a human: "), a suitable likelihood threshold, and normalization/correction for the length of the input and the frequency of its tokens.
